name: Metformin
oneLineAnswer: A prescription pill for type 2 diabetes. It lowers blood sugar by cutting glucose release from your liver.
whatItDoes: Metformin is a biguanide, a drug class used for type 2 diabetes, where blood sugar stays too high.
Metformin tells your liver to release less glucose, the sugar your body burns for fuel.
It also cuts how much glucose your gut absorbs from food.
It helps muscle pull glucose from the blood and respond better to insulin.
It does not make your pancreas release more insulin, and your kidneys clear it unchanged.
whoTheLabelsCover: U.S. tablet labels describe adults who have type 2 diabetes.
The immediate-release tablet label also covers children aged 10 and older.
Metformin comes as tablets, including extended-release tablets, and as a liquid.
Metformin is a medicine rather than a dietary supplement, so the usual supplement sources do not cover it.
whatRecordsShow: In U.S. label trials, the common side effects were diarrhea, nausea or vomiting, gas, indigestion, stomach discomfort, and headache.
The label says metformin can push vitamin B12 below normal. About 7 percent of patients in 29-week trials fell below normal.
NIDDK says most people with type 2 diabetes start with metformin pills.
NIDDK also says the drug may help a person lose a small amount of weight.
Type 2 diabetes treatment can need more than one medicine over time.
safetyFactsRecordedInLabels: The U.S. label carries a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a rare buildup of acid in the blood.
That warning says cases reported after the drug reached the market included deaths.
The label links kidney impairment, certain other medicines, age 65 or older, and heavy alcohol use to that risk.
Liver disease also appears on the label among conditions tied to those acid cases.
The label rules out people with severe kidney impairment, described as an eGFR below 30.
The label flags a higher chance of low blood sugar when metformin is combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea.
The label reports no conclusive evidence that metformin lowers heart attack or stroke risk.
Metformin passes into breast milk, and the label says the effects on a breastfed infant are unknown.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether metformin lowers the risk of heart attack or stroke is not settled.
In one large U.S. trial, metformin cut the chance of developing type 2 diabetes by 31 percent.
Everyone in that trial also got diet and activity advice, so the pill's own share is hard to separate.
No source fetched here reports how much weight or blood sugar change one person would see.
The label found too few older adults in trials to tell whether they respond differently.
Vitamin B12 fell below normal in about 7 percent of patients over 29 weeks. What that means across many years is not established here.
The label says pregnancy data are too limited to settle the risk of birth defects or miscarriage.
Uses outside type 2 diabetes are not covered here. That includes polycystic ovary syndrome and healthy aging claims.

evidence.claim: Metformin is a biguanide labeled for type 2 diabetes, used with diet and exercise, in adults and in children aged 10 and older.
evidence.quote: Metformin is a biguanide indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), indications section of a metformin hydrochloride tablet label

evidence.claim: The extended-release tablet label describes adults only, not children.
evidence.quote: Metformin hydrochloride extended-release tablets is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), same label

evidence.claim: Metformin acts in three named ways: it lowers liver glucose output, lowers glucose absorbed from the gut, and improves insulin sensitivity.
evidence.quote: Metformin decreases hepatic glucose production, decreases intestinal absorption of glucose, and improves insulin sensitivity
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), clinical pharmacology section

evidence.claim: Metformin does not change how much insulin the pancreas secretes, though fasting insulin levels may fall.
evidence.quote: With metformin therapy, insulin secretion remains unchanged while fasting insulin levels and day-long plasma insulin response may decrease.
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), clinical pharmacology section

evidence.claim: NIDDK states the same action in plain words: less glucose from the liver and better insulin use.
evidence.quote: Metformin helps your liver make less glucose and helps your body use insulin better.
evidence.source: NIDDK health information, Insulin, Medicines, & Other Diabetes Treatments

evidence.claim: Metformin is not broken down by the liver and leaves the body in urine unchanged.
evidence.quote: metformin is excreted unchanged in the urine and does not undergo hepatic metabolism
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), pharmacokinetics section of a sitagliptin-metformin label

evidence.claim: The kidney clears metformin, and the label ties kidney impairment to drug accumulation and acid buildup.
evidence.quote: Metformin is substantially excreted by the kidney, and the risk of metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis increases with the degree of renal impairment.
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), use in specific populations section

evidence.claim: The label lists the most common side effects seen above 5 percent in trials.
evidence.quote: the most common adverse reactions (>5.0%) are diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, asthenia, indigestion, abdominal discomfort, and headache
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), adverse reactions section

evidence.claim: The boxed warning describes cases of metformin-associated lactic acidosis reported after marketing that included deaths.
evidence.quote: Postmarketing cases of metformin-associated lactic acidosis have resulted in death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), boxed warning

evidence.claim: The label lists kidney impairment, certain other medicines, and age 65 or older among risk factors for that acid buildup.
evidence.quote: Risk factors for metformin-associated lactic acidosis include renal impairment, concomitant use of certain drugs
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), boxed warning

evidence.claim: Severe kidney impairment, given as an eGFR below 30, is a listed contraindication.
evidence.quote: contraindicated in patients with: Severe renal impairment (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2)
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), contraindications section

evidence.claim: About 7 percent of patients in 29-week trials fell to subnormal vitamin B12 levels.
evidence.quote: a decrease to subnormal levels of previously normal serum vitamin B 12 levels was observed in approximately 7% of patients
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), warnings and precautions section

evidence.claim: The label states there is no conclusive evidence that metformin reduces heart attack or stroke risk.
evidence.quote: There have been no clinical studies establishing conclusive evidence of macrovascular risk reduction
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), warnings and precautions section

evidence.claim: The label raises low blood sugar as a concern when metformin is combined with insulin or an insulin secretagogue such as a sulfonylurea.
evidence.quote: may increase the risk of hypoglycemia when combined with insulin and/or an insulin secretagogue
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), warnings and precautions section

evidence.claim: Alcohol strengthens the effect of metformin on lactate metabolism.
evidence.quote: Alcohol potentiates the effect of metformin on lactate metabolism.
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), warnings and precautions section

evidence.claim: The label associates liver impairment with some cases of lactic acidosis.
evidence.quote: Use of metformin in patients with hepatic impairment has been associated with some cases of lactic acidosis.
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), use in specific populations section

evidence.claim: NIDDK says most people with type 2 diabetes begin treatment with metformin pills.
evidence.quote: Most people with type 2 diabetes start with metformin pills.
evidence.source: NIDDK health information, Insulin, Medicines, & Other Diabetes Treatments

evidence.claim: NIDDK says metformin may help a person lose a small amount of weight.
evidence.quote: This drug may help you lose a small amount of weight.
evidence.source: NIDDK health information, Insulin, Medicines, & Other Diabetes Treatments

evidence.claim: In the Diabetes Prevention Program, metformin lowered the chance of developing type 2 diabetes by 31 percent compared with placebo.
evidence.quote: Participants who took metformin lowered their chances of developing type 2 diabetes by 31 percent compared with participants who took a placebo.
evidence.source: NIDDK, Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP)

evidence.claim: That result came from a randomized controlled trial at 27 U.S. centers between 1996 and 2001.
evidence.quote: The DPP was a randomized, controlled clinical trial conducted at 27 clinical centers around the United States from 1996 to 2001.
evidence.source: NIDDK, Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP)

evidence.claim: The metformin group in that trial also received standard diet and physical activity advice.
evidence.quote: were provided standard advice about diet and physical activity
evidence.source: NIDDK, Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), study design

evidence.claim: PubChem records metformin as compound CID 4091, formula C4H11N5, molecular weight 129.16.
evidence.quote: "CID": 4091, "MolecularFormula": "C4H11N5", "MolecularWeight": "129.16"
evidence.source: PubChem (public domain), compound property table

evidence.claim: A registered trial studies metformin alongside muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function in older adults with type 2 diabetes.
evidence.quote: Metformin in Elderly Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Muscle Strength, Muscle Mass, and Physical Function
evidence.source: ClinicalTrials.gov API v2, study NCT07788378

evidence.claim: Insulin is the hormone that moves glucose into cells.
evidence.quote: A hormone called insulin helps the glucose get into your cells.
evidence.source: MedlinePlus health topic: Diabetes Medicines (public domain)

evidence.claim: In type 2 diabetes the body does not make or use insulin well.
evidence.quote: With type 2 diabetes, your body does not make or use insulin well.
evidence.source: MedlinePlus health topic: Diabetes Medicines (public domain)

evidence.claim: Managing type 2 diabetes can come to need more than one medicine over time.
evidence.quote: Over time, you may need more than one diabetes medicine to manage your blood sugar.
evidence.source: MedlinePlus health topic: Diabetes Medicines (public domain)

evidence.claim: Glucose comes from food and is the fuel body cells use.
evidence.quote: Glucose comes from the foods you eat. The cells of your body need glucose for energy.
evidence.source: MedlinePlus health topic: Diabetes Medicines (public domain)

evidence.claim: Pregnancy data on metformin are too limited to establish a risk of birth defects or miscarriage.
evidence.quote: in pregnant women are not sufficient to determine a drug-associated risk for major birth defects or miscarriage
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), use in specific populations section

evidence.claim: The label says there is not enough information to know the effects of metformin on a breastfed infant.
evidence.quote: there is insufficient information to determine the effects of metformin on the breastfed infant
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), use in specific populations section

evidence.claim: Metformin is present in human milk.
evidence.quote: metformin is present in human milk
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), use in specific populations section

evidence.claim: Trials of these tablets did not include enough older adults to tell whether they respond differently from younger people.
evidence.quote: did not include sufficient numbers of elderly patients to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients
evidence.source: openFDA drug labeling (public domain), use in specific populations section

evidence.claim: Extended-release metformin tablets are made by more than one manufacturer, as indexed in DailyMed.
evidence.quote: "title": "METFORMIN HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET, EXTENDED RELEASE [MACLEODS PHARMACEUTICALS LIMITED]"
evidence.source: DailyMed services API index (public domain)

evidence.claim: Metformin also comes as a liquid.
evidence.quote: Metformin also comes as a liquid.
evidence.source: NIDDK health information, Insulin, Medicines, & Other Diabetes Treatments

gaps: NCCIH has no metformin page. The URL https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/metformin returned HTTP 404, and NCCIH covers dietary supplements rather than prescription drugs, so no NCCIH facts appear here.

A brand-name query for Glucophage on openFDA returned HTTP 404, so no brand-specific label was retrieved. Label facts come from generic metformin hydrochloride tablet labeling plus one sitagliptin-metformin combination label.
Prescription-only status was not quoted from a fetched page. The openFDA record's openfda product-type block was not present in the retrieved text, so that claim is left out rather than assumed.
No numeric blood sugar effect was extracted. The label has a clinical studies section with HbA1c data, but those results were not pulled, so no effect size is stated.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were deliberately excluded as copyrighted. Only the MedlinePlus health topic page was used.

No source fetched here covers metformin in pregnancy for treatment decisions, in polycystic ovary syndrome, or for lifespan and healthy-aging claims. Those uses are ungrounded and are reported only as absent.
The dose used in the Diabetes Prevention Program is on the NIDDK page, but it is not reported here because this page does not report amounts to take.
confidenceRationale: Two independent fetched sources, an FDA prescription-drug label and NIDDK health information, agree on the main claims: the drug class, the type 2 diabetes use, the liver and insulin actions, and the kidney route of removal. A third independent source, MedlinePlus, supports the plain-language background on type 2 diabetes and insulin.

authorship.writtenFor: rnawiki beginner readers who want to know what metformin is and what it does
authorship.method: Facts taken from public-domain U.S. government sources listed above. Every sentence here was written from scratch for rnawiki. No source sentence, table, list order, or heading set was reused.
authorship.limits: Reference content only. It reports what labels and public health pages recorded, and it gives no dosing, no diagnosis, and no treatment advice.
